questions.q: What does a SWAP gate do?
options: It increases a qubit's coherence time
It exchanges the quantum states held by two qubits, letting a compiler relocate information one hop at a time across a connectivity graph
It measures both qubits and resets them to |0>
It permanently deletes the quantum state of one qubit
questions.explain: A SWAP exchanges two qubits' states -- it's how a compiler physically walks information across a chip toward wherever it needs to interact with another qubit.

questions.q: On superconducting hardware, how is a SWAP gate typically implemented, and what does that cost relative to a single native two-qubit gate?
options: As a single native gate with exactly the same cost as one CNOT
As five CNOT gates, making it five times the cost of a native gate
As three CNOT gates in sequence, so each SWAP costs roughly three times the gate count and execution time of a single native two-qubit gate
SWAP gates require no two-qubit interaction at all
questions.explain: SWAP isn't natively implemented -- it's built from three CNOTs (CNOT(A,B), CNOT(B,A), CNOT(A,B)), so every inserted SWAP is really three extra two-qubit gates, each with its own error and time cost.

questions.q: What is a 'SWAP network,' and why do compilers use heuristic (rather than provably optimal) algorithms to build one?
options: It's the full sequence of SWAPs inserted to route a circuit onto a device's connectivity graph; finding the truly optimal sequence is computationally expensive for anything but small circuits, so heuristics trade some optimality for speed
It's a theoretical concept with no real compiler implementation
Heuristics are used because optimal SWAP networks always require zero SWAPs
It's a physical network of wires connecting qubits, unrelated to gate sequences
questions.explain: A SWAP network is the inserted SWAP sequence that makes a circuit's required interactions possible on a given connectivity graph; real compilers use heuristic routing because finding the provably minimal SWAP count is expensive to compute exactly at scale.

questions.q: In the lesson's verified example, a circuit needing 40 native two-qubit gates requires 20 SWAPs to route onto a real device. Roughly how does its total error chance compare with and without that routing overhead, at a representative 0.5% per-gate error rate?
options: About 18% without routing versus about 39% with the 60 extra SWAP-derived gates added -- more than double, with routing responsible for over half the total risk
About 95% without routing versus about 18% with routing, since SWAPs reduce error
About 0.5% in both cases, regardless of total gate count
The error chance is identical either way, since SWAPs don't contribute to circuit error
questions.explain: 1 − (1 − 0.005)^40 is about 18%, while 1 − (1 − 0.005)^100 (40 native + 60 SWAP-derived CNOT-equivalents) is about 39% -- routing overhead alone roughly doubles the circuit's total error risk in this example.

questions.q: Why does connectivity-aware compilation get serious engineering attention rather than being treated as a solved, minor detail?
options: The same logical algorithm can differ substantially in total error and runtime depending on how well it's compiled for a device's connectivity, without the algorithm itself changing at all
Because all compilers produce mathematically identical SWAP networks for any given circuit
Because connectivity-aware compilation has no measurable effect on circuit error
Because SWAP gates are always error-free in practice
questions.explain: Good versus poor routing for the same algorithm on the same device can mean a large difference in total error and runtime purely from SWAP-network quality -- making routing and qubit selection real, practical levers for getting more usable computation out of the same hardware.
